objective_for_doctor: A 32-year-old Female patient presents to the clinic. Chief complaint: I have stridor.

turns.content: Hello, I'm your doctor today. What brings you in today?
Hi doctor. I’m here because I have stridor—like a harsh, noisy breathing sound. It started after I had a cold in the last two weeks, and I’m also a current cigarette smoker.
Doctor: I’m Dr. Agent—first, is the stridor mainly when you inhale (upper/neck noise) or when you exhale? Also, do you have any drooling, trouble swallowing, fever, or a change in voice (hoarseness)?
It’s mainly when I inhale, like a noise from my throat/neck. I don’t have drooling, trouble swallowing, fever, or a change in my voice/hoarseness.

Doctor: Any history of choking episodes, worsening over hours vs days, and do you feel short of breath even at rest? Also, can you tolerate lying flat and have you ever had similar episodes or known allergies?

No choking episodes that I know of. It feels like it’s been going on over the last day or so and not like it slowly got worse over days. I do feel short of breath, even at rest, and I can’t lie flat comfortably. I’ve had similar breathing problems before, and I do have asthma—I’ve used a bronchodilator before. I don’t know of any known allergies.

Doctor: I’m concerned about an upper-airway cause given your inspiratory stridor plus shortness of breath at rest and inability to lie flat—do you have any severe throat pain, muffled “hot potato” voice, neck swelling, or do you hear any wheeze as well? Also, have you been able to speak full sentences without stopping for breath?

No severe throat pain, and I don’t have neck swelling. I don’t think my voice is muffled like that “hot potato” sound. I do sometimes wheeze because of my asthma. I’m not able to speak full sentences—I have to stop for breath.

Doctor: I’m going to act carefully—can you tell me if you have any measurable relief with your asthma inhaler, and do you have a pulse oximeter reading if available? Also, I need a quick safety check: are you currently struggling to breathe, blue lips, or unable to speak more than a few words?
I haven’t had much relief with my inhaler today, so far. I don’t have a pulse oximeter reading. Right now I’m struggling to breathe and I can only say a few words before I need to stop.

Doctor: I’m very concerned you may have a serious upper-airway problem or impending respiratory failure—this needs urgent assessment; are you alone right now, and do you have someone who can take you to the ER immediately or call emergency services? Also, can you tell me your current temperature and whether the stridor is getting rapidly worse over the last hour?
I’m alone right now. I can get someone to take me to the ER immediately, but I need to call them. I don’t know my temperature. The stridor feels like it’s getting worse over the last hour.

Doctor: Please call emergency services or have someone take you to the ER immediately—your symptoms (inspiratory stridor, difficulty speaking full sentences, worsening over the last hour, and poor response to inhaler) suggest a potentially life-threatening upper-airway obstruction. Do you have a pulse oximeter or can you check and tell me your oxygen saturation right now, and can you start moving toward the exit while someone drives you?
I don’t have a pulse oximeter. I’ll move toward the exit now and I’ll get someone to drive me to the ER right away.

Doctor: I’m Dr. Agent—while you’re arranging the ER, I need one more safety check: on a scale of 0–10 how bad is your breathing right now, and are you able to take even one full breath in without significant pause or worsening stridor?  
Doctor: Also, if you have access, REQUEST TEST: Portable_pulse_ox (bring it to measure SpO₂ on arrival).

My breathing feels about a 8/10 right now. I can’t take one full breath without a big pause and it gets worse with the stridor. I don’t have a pulse oximeter, but I’ll request one on arrival and ask them to measure my SpO₂.

Doctor: I’m very concerned you’re at risk for an acute upper-airway obstruction/impending respiratory failure—this is an emergency; are you currently on your way to the ER now (and can you confirm your weight/any pregnancy possibility)?  
Doctor: While you’re traveling, REQUEST TEST: Continuous_pulse_ox/O2_saturation_on_arrival.
I’m on my way to the ER now. I don’t know my weight right now, and there’s no pregnancy possibility that I’m aware of. I’ll ask for continuous pulse ox and oxygen saturation on arrival.

Doctor: I’m Dr. Agent—thank you; focus on getting to the ER immediately and tell them you have **inspiratory stridor**, **can’t speak full sentences**, **worsening over the last hour**, and **minimal bronchodilator relief**, and ask for **rapid evaluation of upper-airway obstruction**.  
Doctor: On arrival, request **REQUEST TEST: ENT_airway_evaluation (flexible_laryngoscopy as indicated)** and **REQUEST TEST: CBC_CMP** plus **REQUEST TEST: Neck_Chest_Xray** (or CT airway if they think it’s needed).  
DIAGNOSIS READY: Acute upper-airway obstruction with impending respiratory failure—most consistent with **laryngeal obstruction/upper-airway edema or mass (e.g., viral laryngitis/edema, croup-like presentation, or other laryngeal pathology)**; needs emergency airway assessment.

[DDX]
1. Croup
